item.title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
item.description:
Explainer
Voting
Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
October 28, 20265:00 AM ET
Hansi Lo Wang
Students at the University of Virginia help eligible voters register to vote in Charlottesville, Va., in 2024.
Ryan M. Kelly/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Ryan M. Kelly/AP
Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?
A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.
That issue resurfaced in discussions about changes Montana made last year to its requirements for residents who want to register to vote. After a student advocacy group sued, a state judge blocked the new restriction for now. That leaves the previous rules in place for Montana students who want to register to vote, including for the midterm elections through Election Day.

October 28, 20265:00 AM ET

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event on October 17, 2026 in Marietta, Georgia.
Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images

Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App
In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.
An NPR analysis of Google Ads for four major Senate races — Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas — found that the Democratic and Republican candidates spent more than $15 million on advertising related to fundraising in the 2025-26 election cycle. About three quarters of that went to ads that ran nationally.
Loading...
Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

item.title: Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds
item.description:
Immigration
Partnerships between ICE and local police surge, report finds
October 28, 20265:00 AM ET
Jaclyn Diaz
Federal agents walk near the scene where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during an operation in the Bronx borough of New York on Oct. 8, 2026.
Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images
The number of state and local officers working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement has doubled in size in the last eight months, according to a new report from the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us.
The group analyzed the federal ICE program, called 287(g), that deputizes state and local police for immigration enforcement. It used the agency's public records and information requested by the Deportation Data Project, which is based at UC Berkeley and UCLA and collects U.S. immigration enforcement data.
More than 29,000 officers were deputized by ICE between January 2025 and October 2026. That's far more than the 11,600 deportation officers directly employed by ICE.

item.description:

A U.S. cruise ship ends voyage due to fuel costs and passengers lose their homes
October 28, 20263:57 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026.
Heng Sinith/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Heng Sinith/AP
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," it said. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.

item.title: Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling
item.description:
Climate
Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling
October 28, 20262:15 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
President Donald Trump throws a hat into the crowd as he arrives at a campaign rally at Lubbock Memorial Civic Center, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas.
Annie Rice/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Annie Rice/AP
BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.
Climate
U.N. climate report warns world will soon cross a dangerous threshold
Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil. That's equivalent to about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.
The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.
Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.
